section_summary: This section examines Japan’s foreign exchange resources during the war in China, including gold reserves, overseas balances, securities, trade deficits and possible loans. It also documents American firms’ difficulty obtaining dollars from yen held in Japan, especially for cotton transactions and a Ford Motor Company dividend. State Department correspondence records requests for assistance, consular warnings and tighter Japanese exchange controls.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Ultimate Foreign Exchange Resources
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s capacity to finance a prolonged war through gold, foreign securities, trade and borrowing.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum estimates theoretical resources near six billion yen but liquid or convertible resources near two billion. It reviews gold reserves and production, overseas bank balances, foreign securities, investments and a growing trade deficit. It concludes that available exchange could support Japan for at least a year, while foreign loans could extend that period.

subfiles.title: Orvis letter enclosing memorandum on blocked yen
subfiles.about: Encloses an explanation of yen deposits needed to reimburse cotton futures margin payments.
subfiles.summary: Orvis asks to be advised of any action on his firm’s blocked funds.

subfiles.title: Position of Japanese firms with New York cotton futures contracts
subfiles.about: Explains how delayed Japanese exchange permits burden Orvis Brothers’ cotton hedge accounts.
subfiles.summary: Japanese textile manufacturers and merchants bought New York cotton futures to hedge forward sales. After cotton prices fell, their yen margin deposits in Osaka could not be converted into dollars, forcing Orvis Brothers to cover daily clearing requirements with its own funds. The firm asks the Department to raise the prolonged delay with Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Reply to Orvis on blocked funds
subfiles.about: Reports that the American Embassy in Tokyo has been asked to inquire about delayed exchange permits.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton promises to relay information received from the Embassy.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ambassador Grew concerning Orvis Brothers
subfiles.from: Francis B. Sayre, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests a Foreign Office inquiry into delayed permission to transfer Orvis Brothers’ funds.
subfiles.summary: The Department describes the cotton futures margin problem and its policy on assistance to private interests with frozen funds. Grew is asked to inquire when Japan’s Exchange Control Commission expects to act.

subfiles.title: Orvis memorandum enclosed with diplomatic instruction
subfiles.from: Orvis Brothers & Co.; Homer W. Orvis
subfiles.about: Provides the Embassy a copy of Orvis Brothers’ explanation of blocked cotton hedge margin.
subfiles.summary: The copy recounts Japanese clients’ hedging, yen deposits in Osaka and Orvis Brothers’ dollar obligations to the cotton clearing association. It asks for help securing conversion permits.

subfiles.title: Notice to Orvis of exchange permits granted
subfiles.about: Reports that Japan granted permits to transfer 281,000 yen to Orvis’s correspondents.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports exchange permits covering 281,000 yen.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Homer W. Orvis about blocked funds
subfiles.about: Records Orvis’s account of blocked cotton futures margin payments and his request for assistance.
subfiles.summary: Orvis says about $200,000 in yen margin deposits cannot be converted, though he must provide matching dollars in New York. Officials ask him to submit the case in writing and discuss possible inquiries in Tokyo and Washington.

subfiles.title: Embassy letter requesting appraisal of Japanese external resources
subfiles.about: Requests the promised appraisal for discussion with the British Treasury.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth asks that it cover Japan’s short-term money market facilities.

subfiles.title: Feis letter forwarding Japanese exchange resource memoranda
subfiles.about: Forwards two working memoranda for comparison with British Treasury estimates.
subfiles.summary: Feis requests British comments and any information it can share.

subfiles.title: Supplement to Japan’s Ultimate Foreign Exchange Resources
subfiles.about: Updates estimates of Japanese gold shipments, remaining gold and bank balances.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page revises figures for gold and Japanese balances in the United States.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Ford representatives about funds blocked in Japan
subfiles.about: Records Ford Motor Company’s inquiry about dividend and shipment payments held in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ford representatives describe a dividend of roughly three and a half million yen and unpaid materials shipments. Jones outlines ways to request State Department or Embassy assistance.

subfiles.title: Protection of American Exporters of Cotton to Osaka
subfiles.from: Kenneth C. Krentz, American Consul, Osaka
subfiles.about: Warns American cotton exporters that Japanese exchange controls have frozen payments.
subfiles.summary: Krentz estimates ten to twelve million yen owed to foreign cotton shippers is frozen, most of it due to Americans. He describes declining Osaka cotton stocks, pressure to ship on credit and the limited value of import certificates. He advises against shipment without full advance settlement.

subfiles.title: Osaka telegram on Dixon cotton shipment at Kobe
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for R. L. Dixon and Brother
subfiles.about: Relays the prospect of permits for a cotton shipment held at Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Nishikawa and Kato expect permits may become available after September 20.

subfiles.title: Department forwarding Osaka telegram to Dixon
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of Foreign Service Administration
subfiles.about: Forwards the consul’s message about cotton held at Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats the consul’s report that permits may follow September 20.

subfiles.title: Dixon acknowledgment concerning cotton shipment
subfiles.about: Thanks the Department and explains the loss caused by delayed payment for cotton.
subfiles.summary: Dixon says the May shipment remains unpaid while cotton prices have fallen.

subfiles.title: Feis note on Japanese exchange resources report
subfiles.about: Introduces a checked estimate of Japan’s foreign exchange resources.
subfiles.summary: Feis plans to share an edited copy with Sir Frederick Phillips.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Ultimate Foreign Exchange Resources
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s liquid and theoretical foreign exchange resources as war spending rises.
subfiles.summary: This clearer copy of the memorandum on pages 1–11 values Japan’s theoretical resources at about six billion yen and liquid or convertible resources at about two billion. It examines gold, bank balances, foreign securities, investments, trade and possible loans. Its conclusion is that Japan could finance deficits for at least a year, perhaps longer with increasing difficulty or foreign borrowing.

subfiles.title: Osaka telegram on cotton importers’ dollar exchange
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for R. L. Dixon and Brother
subfiles.about: Reports that dollar exchange remains unavailable to cotton importers.
subfiles.summary: Kato expects a remittance permit the following week.

subfiles.title: Department telegram to Dixon
subfiles.about: Forwards Osaka’s report on dollar exchange for cotton importers.
subfiles.summary: The Department repeats Kato’s expectation of a permit.

subfiles.title: Osaka warning on cotton import exchange restrictions
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese controls may leave much cotton payment frozen in yen.
subfiles.summary: Bankers and cotton merchants recommend shipping only against confirmed credits.

subfiles.title: Dixon acknowledgment of Department telegram
subfiles.about: Thanks the Department for its prompt help concerning payment from a Japanese buyer.
subfiles.summary: Dixon acknowledges the Osaka consul’s message about payment due from Ketoh & Co.

subfiles.title: Osaka telegram on continued absence of cotton exchange permits
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for R. L. Dixon and Brothers
subfiles.about: Reports that no cotton exchange permits were issued in October or November.
subfiles.summary: Krentz urges precautions because Nishikawa has no assurance of payment.

subfiles.title: Department telegram forwarding Osaka warning
subfiles.about: Forwards the consul’s warning about continued nonissuance of cotton exchange permits.
subfiles.summary: The Department relays Krentz’s advice to take full precautions.

subfiles.title: Ford Motor Company request for assistance with dividend
subfiles.from: Ford Motor Company, General Sales Department
subfiles.about: Requests Embassy assistance in remitting a dividend from Ford Motor Company of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ford seeks transfer of a dividend totaling $887,088.46.

subfiles.title: Ford Motor Company of Japan Limited dividend
subfiles.about: Lists dividend amounts, tax and net payments for Ford’s American shareholders.
subfiles.summary: The net foreign shareholder payment is $887,088.46.

subfiles.title: Ford correspondence envelope
subfiles.about: Envelope associated with Ford’s request for assistance.
subfiles.summary: Addressed to the State Department in Washington.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Ford Motor Company
subfiles.about: Reports that the Embassy has been asked to inquire about Ford’s delayed dividend transfer.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the Embassy will seek information from the Foreign Office on when exchange permit applications will be decided.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ambassador Grew concerning Ford funds
subfiles.from: Francis B. Sayre, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs an inquiry into exchange permission for Ford’s $887,088.46 dividend.
subfiles.summary: The Department distinguishes Ford’s dividend request from its earlier concern over payment for shipped parts, which Ford no longer wishes to pursue. Grew is asked to consult Ford’s manager in Japan, then raise the permit delay with the Foreign Office if appropriate.

subfiles.title: Follow-up conversation with Ford representatives
subfiles.about: Records Ford’s formal request for help transferring its Japanese dividend.
subfiles.summary: Connolly and Poore submit Ford’s letter requesting assistance with $887,088.46. They decline to have the Japanese branch approach the Embassy and withdraw the earlier request concerning payment for shipped materials.

subfiles.title: Conversation on Japanese bank balances in New York
subfiles.about: Records Treasury figures for Japanese bank balances in New York.
subfiles.summary: Lochhead reports $45 million in balances on November 24, four-fifths at the Yokohama Specie Bank’s New York branch. The memorandum suggests recent gold shipments may have built reserves.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on strengthened exchange controls
subfiles.about: Reports new Japanese permit and reporting requirements for overseas assets and remittances.
subfiles.summary: The Finance Ministry extends controls over overseas property transactions by Japanese subjects, requires reports on holdings and transactions, and lowers the amounts that may be remitted abroad without permits.

subfiles.title: Cover letter enclosing Treasury memoranda
subfiles.about: Encloses memoranda on Japan’s exchange reserves and current trade with Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The cover letter identifies two enclosed Treasury analyses.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Foreign Exchange Resources and Reserves
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s available exchange and its capacity to sustain war, including a possible conflict with the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum estimates at least $475 million in convertible assets and suggests Japan could continue operations at the current scale for roughly another year. It distinguishes readily available funds from gold reserves and other assets that could be mobilized under pressure, while estimating exchange use at $30–40 million monthly. The surviving pages detail gold holdings, foreign balances and securities, and begin a discussion of Japanese foreign currency obligations; the document continues beyond page 80.
